stated: Reform UK will target 70% 'Buy British' to ensure food security, mandate taxpayer-funded organisations to source 75% of their food from the UK, implement clear labelling for consumer choice, and boost smaller food processors and abattoirs through tax breaks.

source.quote: Buy British. Buy Quality Target 70% to ensure food security. Taxpayer funded organisations should source 75% of their food from the UK. Clear labelling for consumer choice. Boost smaller food processors and abattoirs through tax breaks and other incentives.

bearing_set.reason: Mandating domestic sourcing (70–75%) could raise food prices if UK produce costs more than imports — food costs are a direct O2 indicator, making this a real verdict on household affordability.
Tax breaks for smaller food processors and abattoirs directly affect job viability and employment levels in rural food-industry sectors — a non-negligible effect on job quality and security.
The policy is explicitly framed around food security as national resilience; supply-chain self-sufficiency maps directly to the O5 indicator 'resilience to external threats'.

Requiring taxpayer-funded organisations to procure more expensive domestically-sourced food raises public procurement costs; tax breaks for processors and abattoirs reduce Exchequer revenue — both worsen the funded/borrowed balance.

Restricting import competition reduces allocative efficiency and raises the risk of trade retaliation, while domestic food-industry incentives could lift sectoral investment — creating a contested net effect on productivity and real living standards.

Higher food prices from the domestic-sourcing mandate fall disproportionately on lower-income households, who spend a larger share of income on food, widening the consumption gap — an inequality effect distinct from O2's absolute-price concern.

membership_note: Five fundamentals earn a real verdict: O2 (food price rises), O5 (food-security resilience), O12 (fiscal costs of mandate and tax breaks), O13 (trade efficiency vs domestic industry tradeoff), and O14 (regressive distributional food-price effect). Labelling reform alone would be negligible, but it is not the only or dominant component.
